questions.prompt: What is the main goal of the ordinary-extraordinary strategy?
choices: Break the opponent's forecast of the next move
Convince the opponent that you are morally superior
Hide the true facts of the situation

explanation.gentle: The chapter centers on expectation because the operator is trying to make the opponent's prediction fail.
explanation.direct: Begin with the job: the strategy targets forecast, not truth or moral posture.
explanation.competitive: At the sharpest level, the move wins by denying the enemy a usable pattern.

questions.prompt: When can the ordinary move be the strongest choice?
choices: When the extraordinary move has become expected
When the operator wants to appear humble
When the field does not contain any real pressure

explanation.gentle: Sometimes plainness is the least expected texture in the room.
explanation.direct: Keep in view the logic: if spectacle is expected, ordinary can be the deeper cut.
explanation.competitive: The cold reading is simple: once drama is priced in, calm becomes asymmetric.

questions.prompt: What is the chapter's main reversal about unpredictability?
choices: It works only in school settings
It becomes destructive when it turns into randomness without a stable objective
It always requires a dramatic public gesture

explanation.gentle: The chapter warns that variation without an anchor damages the operator first.
explanation.direct: Notice the cost: unpredictability becomes noise when the stable aim disappears.
explanation.competitive: The reversal is brutal because chaos taxes your own side before it hurts anyone else.

questions.prompt: Junia sees that the counterparty expects one more late dramatic escalation. What fits the chapter best?
choices: Make the ordinary request that breaks the forecast
Double the drama so the counterparty knows you are serious
Delay any move until the counterparty speaks first

explanation.gentle: Junia succeeds by choosing the move the room is least prepared to process.
explanation.direct: In Junia's case, the quiet move works because the dramatic one has become too legible.
explanation.competitive: Her edge comes from letting the other side overprepare for the wrong beat.

questions.prompt: Kester says randomness and disciplined unpredictability are opposites. What is his key distinction?
choices: Randomness uses more courage than planning
Disciplined unpredictability keeps a stable objective while texture changes
Disciplined unpredictability avoids all ordinary moves

explanation.gentle: Kester keeps the strategy anchored to a fixed aim instead of to erratic behavior.
explanation.direct: Kester's test is whether the objective remains stable while cadence or form shifts.
explanation.competitive: He splits strategy from chaos by asking what stays fixed beneath the variance.

questions.prompt: Aislin wants to change her meeting cadence because the vendor has memorized her normal script. What should guide the decision?
choices: Whether the change will look bold to her team
Whether the change is the most emotionally intense option
Whether the change serves the same objective better than the old pattern does

explanation.gentle: A cadence shift is only strategic if it improves the same underlying job.
explanation.direct: Look at the objective first. If the new texture serves the same aim better, use it.
explanation.competitive: The move is justified by forecast failure tied to purpose, not by appetite for novelty.

questions.prompt: Bodie is in a personal conflict where trust depends on steadiness. Which choice matches the chapter?
choices: Become harder to read so the other person loses leverage
Keep the reliable commitment because predictability is part of the value here
Alternate between warmth and silence to regain emotional initiative

explanation.gentle: This example exists to show where the strategy should be restrained.
explanation.direct: Here reliability wins because the relationship depends on steadiness more than on tactical asymmetry.
explanation.competitive: If trust is the asset, variation is the wrong weapon.

questions.prompt: Renata's rival is intercepting her campaign rhythm because her posts always land at the same time. What is the best response?
choices: Post even more often at the same time so supporters can rely on it
Change cadence selectively while keeping the campaign logic coherent
Stop posting altogether until the rival gets bored

explanation.gentle: Renata needs variance with continuity, not panic.
explanation.direct: A usable sign is selective cadence change that breaks interception without scrambling the campaign.
explanation.competitive: The right fix is controlled variance, not surrender and not rigid repetition.

questions.prompt: Which judgment best captures the chapter's limit?
choices: Any surprising move is strategic if it confuses the other side
Only extraordinary moves create real leverage
Variation is useful only when it interrupts exploitation without destroying internal coherence

explanation.gentle: The chapter rejects both theatrical surprise and mechanical consistency as universal answers.
explanation.direct: The limit appears where variance starts harming your own coordination more than the opponent's forecast.
explanation.competitive: The serious measure is whether the move breaks exploitation while preserving your own design.

questions.prompt: How does Chapter 24 differ from Chapter 25?
choices: Chapter 24 focuses on moral sympathy, while Chapter 25 focuses on timing
Chapter 24 is about exiting on time, while Chapter 25 is about inner sabotage
Chapter 24 breaks expectation inside the contest, while Chapter 25 seeks advantage through third-party judgment

explanation.gentle: Chapter 24 and Chapter 25 work on different audiences.
explanation.direct: Separate the jobs: one chapter scrambles forecast, the next recruits observers through moral positioning.
explanation.competitive: The difference is internal expectation versus external legitimacy.
